proposal: The Mandate says a conservative administration should state that no new direct lending programs will be developed at the SBA and should aim for an end to SBA direct lending. It also recommends working with Congress to assess whether disaster loans should be offered by another agency rather than the SBA and exploring private-sector channels, citing overlap with FEMA aid, weaker incentives to buy insurance, and the fact that more than 90 percent of disaster loans go to individuals rather than businesses.
remaining: A public commitment that SBA will create no new direct lending programs (none found).

status_summary: No action ending SBA direct lending, stating that SBA will develop no new direct lending programs, or moving disaster lending to another agency or private channel was found as of 2026-10-08. SBA is operating and adjusting its direct disaster loan program: its Associate Administrator for Disaster Recovery told a House committee on 2025-12-16 that SBA had approved 27,996 disaster loans totaling about $4.76 billion since 2025-01-20 and was moving the lending function into the Office of Disaster Recovery and Resilience; an interim final rule published 2026-01-29 (91 FR 3813) preempts state and local permit delays over 60 days so borrowers can use approved funds; and SBA's disaster page (last modified 2026-10-01) lists loans for Hawaii, Alaska and California disasters. GAO reported on 2026-05-18 that the program supported about $1.7 billion in lending and more than 27,000 direct loans in FY2024. The FEMA Review Council's final report (approved 2026-05-07) recommends shifting disaster responsibilities toward states and private insurers, but the CRS summary and two press summaries read do not mention SBA disaster loans. The FY2027 SBA request (per CRS, 2026-05-27) would cut the disaster loan program to $143 million from $282 million in FY2026 and end funding for most entrepreneurial development programs; CRS describes no proposal to end or transfer direct lending.

timeline.event: A presidential document on California water and disaster response directs the SBA Administrator, with other officials, to support recovery for North Carolina families, showing a continued SBA disaster role.

SBA's Associate Administrator for the Office of Disaster Recovery and Resilience testifies to the House Committee on Small Business that since 2025-01-20 SBA has approved 27,996 disaster loans totaling about $4.76 billion (64 percent more than the same period of 2024), cut average approval time to 15.4 days, and is moving the disaster lending function back into his office. The testimony does not mention moving the program to another agency or to private lenders (SBA's own figures, not independently checked).
timeline.source: House Committee on Small Business (testimony as posted by the committee's Democratic staff)

timeline.event: SBA publishes an interim final rule, 'Improving SBA Disaster Loan Ability To Provide Meaningful and Timely Assistance' (91 FR 3813), adding 13 CFR part 123 subpart I to preempt state and local requirements that cause permit delays of more than 60 days in work financed by SBA disaster loans; effective the same day, comments due 2026-03-02. SBA cites slow disbursement after the January 2025 California wildfires. The rule does not address who delivers the loans.

The FEMA Review Council approves its final report; a CRS summary (2026-05-15) lists recommendations including up-front formula grants to states for Public Assistance, a single payment for survivors with uninhabitable homes, and moving flood insurance toward private insurers, with no mention of SBA disaster loans, direct loans or private lending.

GAO report GAO-26-108688 on the SBA disaster loan program (about $1.7 billion in lending and more than 27,000 direct disaster loans in FY2024) recommends consistent outreach to survivors; SBA neither agreed nor disagreed. It does not discuss moving the program.

CRS summarizes the administration's FY2027 SBA request: $329.0 million in new discretionary funding (down 74.7 percent), disaster loan program funding of $143.0 million versus $282.0 million in FY2026, zero for nearly all entrepreneurial development programs, and a proposed lender fee in the 7(a), 504 and SBIC programs to offset administrative costs; no proposal to end, transfer or privatize direct or disaster lending is described.

SBA's disaster page (last-modified date) states the agency is offering loans for multiple declared disasters (Hawaii severe storms, Alaska floods, California wildfires), with no notice of a pause, transfer or phase-out.

title: End SBA direct lending and explore moving disaster loans to other agencies or lenders
uncertainties: Absence-of-evidence finding. The FEMA Review Council report itself and the SBA FY2027 budget justification were not read directly (neither was found on a fetchable page); the first is known from a CRS summary and two press summaries (National League of Cities, Housing Assistance Council) that do not mention SBA, and the second from a CRS Insight, so a recommendation or budget line on SBA disaster loans could sit in the full documents. CRS did not split the $143 million disaster funding into subsidy and administrative parts, and the reason for the proposed cut was not given. Bills in Congress to move disaster lending were searched for in two web searches that returned only older material; none was found. The testimony figures are SBA's own. A Federal Register query for SBA documents mentioning direct loans returned only quarterly interest rate notices. Judgment: the SBA is continuing and speeding up the direct disaster loan program, which a reviewer could classify as diverged from the Mandate's goal of ending direct lending; not_started is used because no step toward or explicit reversal of the recommendation was found and the FY2027 request halves the program's funding. Searches run this pass: SBA disaster loan program moved to FEMA, Treasury or private lenders (2026); FEMA Review Council final report and SBA; Loeffler and SBA disaster loan changes; House Small Business Committee disaster loan bills. Plus direct fetches of the SBA disaster page, GAO-26-108688, CRS IN12693 and IN12694, and the Federal Register.
